lesson.title: Hobbys II: die Party, die Gitarre, reiten, das Schach, die Freizeit
lesson.subtitle: the party set — a Persian king, a Greek harp, and the free time you already speak

hook.title: The King's Game, the Kithara, and Free Time
hook.content: The past-time set, and every word is a passport stamp. die Party is English party bought back — and English party is Old French partie, 'a part, a side': first the people on your side, then the gathering itself. die Gitarre took the grand tour: Spanish guitarra, on loan from Greek kithara, the concert lyre of Apollo — and English guitar is the same Spanish purchase, so the word crossed the Mediterranean twice and landed in both languages. reiten is the native one, and it conjugates strong: reiten, ritt, geritten — ride, rode, ridden — the same vowel-ablaut both languages inherited, still turning on the same hinge. das Schach is royalty in hiding: Persian shāh, 'king', carried through Arabic into French échec and German Schach — and when you say checkmate, you are saying the Persian sentence shāh māt, 'the king is helpless'. Check, Schach, checkmate: one king, three coins. And die Freizeit is the compound engine at full power: frei + Zeit — frei is English free, and Zeit is English tide in its older meaning of 'time' (time and tide wait for no man). German glues it on and builds Freizeitpark, Freizeitstress, Freizeitprogramm — free time as an industry.

footnotes.title: The Zither Cousin
footnotes.content: English zither is the same Greek kithara that built die Gitarre — it came through Latin cithara into German die Zither, and English bought it from German. Guitar, Gitarre, zither: one Greek lyre, three descendants.

pattern.title: Invited to the Party
pattern.content: 1. reiten runs strong: ich reite, du reitest, er reitet — ritt — geritten; the vowel changes with the tense, exactly like ride/rode/ridden. 2. The frames: Das Schach ist mein Hobby, Wir tanzen auf der Party, Die Musik auf der Party kommt aus dem Radio. 3. The compound: die Freizeit = frei + Zeit, and German keeps gluing: der Freizeitpark, der Freizeitstress. 4. The logistics: Mit dem Taxi zur Party, Wir gehen ins Theater, Vor der Party kommt der Friseur. 5. endlich lands where the joy is: Endlich kommt die Freizeit — finally, the weekend.
pattern.linguist_note: Schach is the oldest word in the room. When the Arabic-speaking world learned chess from Persia, it kept the king's title — shāh — and Europe borrowed the Arabic form as French eschec, German Schach, English check. The game's most feared word, checkmate, is the Persian sentence shāh māt, 'the king is helpless': the game ends when the king has no move left, and the etymology says exactly that.

exercises.prompt: The party begins — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The music at the party comes from the radio
matching_pairs.german: Die Musik auf der Party kommt aus dem Radio

matching_pairs.english: The piano is old, the guitar is new
matching_pairs.german: Das Klavier ist alt, die Gitarre ist neu

matching_pairs.english: Before the party comes the hairdresser
matching_pairs.german: Vor der Party kommt der Friseur

matching_pairs.english: The singer at the party sings a song
matching_pairs.german: Der Sänger auf der Party singt ein Lied

matching_pairs.english: Sport on TV, music at the party
matching_pairs.german: Sport im Fernsehen, Musik auf der Party

matching_pairs.english: My free time: chess and music
Rolls and toast at the party
matching_pairs.german: Brötchen und Toast auf der Party

exercises.target_answer: Die Musik auf der Party kommt aus dem Radio, Das Klavier ist alt, die Gitarre ist neu, Mit dem Taxi zur Party, Vor der Party kommt der Friseur, Musik ist mein Beruf, Der Sänger auf der Party singt ein Lied, Das Schach ist mein Hobby, Der Bauer reitet, Sport im Fernsehen, Musik auf der Party, Meine Freizeit: Schach und Musik, Brötchen und Toast auf der Party, Malen ist mein Hobby
exercises.meaning: party, guitar, riding, chess, free time — the invitation
exercises.explanation: One invitation, in sentences. auf der Party is where the music lives, zur Party is how you travel — German splits 'at' and 'to' where English uses one word. The old words attend too: der Bauer reitet, der Sänger singt, Brötchen und Toast wait on the table.

exercises.prompt: Which of today's five hobby verbs is a strong verb meaning 'to ride on horseback' (cognate with English ride, rode, ridden)?
exercises.meaning: reiten is the strong verb: the same ablaut as ride/rode/ridden
exercises.explanation: die Party, das Schach and die Freizeit are borrowed or built. reiten is the inherited verb, and its vowel dance — reiten, ritt, geritten — is the same ablaut English rides through in ride, rode, ridden.

exercises.prompt: 'die Gitarre' and its English twin took the same road: Spanish guitarra, from Greek kithara. Give the English twin:
exercises.meaning: die Gitarre ↔ guitar: one Greek lyre, two languages
exercises.explanation: Spanish guitarra came from Greek kithara, and both German and English bought it from Spanish. harp is a Germanic word (German Harfe) for a different instrument, so it is not a twin.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the dancing sentence: 'We dance at the party'
exercises.explanation: auf + dative der Party — at the party, the location. The Kino and Musik tiles belong to other evenings; the frame stays.
exercises.affirmation: Auf der Party the location and the fun share one preposition.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the Friday feeling: 'Finally the free time comes'
exercises.explanation: endlich — finally — is the little word that opens the weekend: Endlich kommt die Freizeit. And die Freizeit is a compound you can already read: frei (free) + Zeit (tide, in its old meaning of time).
exercises.affirmation: Freizeit is two words you own, glued into one you can read.

summary.outcome: Talk about parties, guitars, riding, chess and free time — and hear the Persian king inside checkmate.

use_example.german: Endlich kommt die Freizeit — wir tanzen auf der Party.
use_example.english: Finally the free time comes — we dance at the party.

summary.takeaway: die Gitarre and guitar share a Greek kithara, das Schach is the Persian shāh, reiten ritt geritten is ride rode ridden — and die Freizeit is free + tide.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the people around the music — wir, die Schule, der Gast, die Gruppe, der Held.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Hobbys II: die Party, die Gitarre, reiten, das Schach, die Freizeit (Finally the free time comes):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Endlich kommt die Freizeit" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Hobbys II: die Party, die Gitarre, reiten, das Schach, die Freizeit without relying on short-term echo.

party.etymology_derivation: Unadapted borrowing from English party — a doublet of older loans Partei/Partie. [wiktionary]

gitarre.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Spanish guitarra, from Arabic qithara, from Greek kithara - the same Spanish word that gave English guitar. [wiktionary]

reiten.context_translation: The child is learning to ride.
reiten.etymology_derivation: Class 1 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną - the exact twin of English ride: reiten-ritt-geritten matches ride-rode-ridden. [wiktionary]

schach.etymology_derivation: From Arabic shah, from Persian shah (king) - the same word that gave English check and checkmate (Persian shah mat, the king is dead). [wiktionary][etymonline]

freizeit.context_phrase: In meiner Freizeit lese ich Bücher.
freizeit.context_translation: In my free time I read books.
freizeit.etymology_derivation: frei + Zeit, literally free time; frei is the exact twin of free and Zeit the twin of time (as in tide, t to z). [wiktionary]

endlich.etymology_derivation: Ende + -lich, a formation the page itself compares to English endly; Ende is the documented twin of end. [wiktionary]

radio.context_translation: We listen to the radio in the car.
radio.etymology_derivation: Borrowed about 1920 from English radio, short for radiotelegraphy - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

klavier.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French clavier, from Latin clavis 'key' — a Romance loan. [wiktionary]

hobby.etymology_derivation: An unadapted borrowing of English hobby — the same word, kept with German spelling and plural Hobbys. [wiktionary]

taxi.context_phrase: Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Hotel.
taxi.context_translation: We take a taxi to the hotel.
taxi.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French taxi, the cab named for its taximeter — the identical French word English uses. [wiktionary]

theater.context_translation: We are going to the theater today.
theater.etymology_derivation: From French théâtre, from Latin theātrum, from Greek theātron (a place for viewing) — the same viewing-place word English took as theater. [wiktionary]

friseur.etymology_derivation: A French-style formation from frisieren; no standard English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

beruf.etymology_derivation: Literally the calling, deverbal of berufen (to call) - the same idea as English vocation (Latin vocare, to call), though the words are unrelated. [wiktionary]

sänger.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of singen (sing); initial s voices to [z] before vowels. [wiktionary]

sport.etymology_derivation: 19th-century borrowing from English sport — see treiben (to drive) in Ich treibe Sport. [wiktionary]

musik.etymology_derivation: From Latin mūsica — the same Latin loan as English music. [wiktionary]

lied.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *leuþ 'song'; no modern English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

tanzen.etymology_derivation: From Old French dancer via Low German — the same French loan as English dance. [wiktionary]

schokolade.context_phrase: Die Schokolade ist für die Kinder.
schokolade.context_translation: The chocolate is for the children.
schokolade.etymology_derivation: Schokolade — borrowed via Dutch chocolade from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl; English chocolate comes from the same Spanish word. [wiktionary]

keks.context_phrase: Ich nehme einen Keks zum Kaffee.
keks.context_translation: I am taking a cookie with my coffee.
keks.etymology_derivation: Keks — a 1900s borrowing of English cakes, popularized when Bahlsen renamed Leibniz-Cakes to Leibniz-Keks in 1911; northern German uses der, the south often das. [wiktionary]

torte.context_phrase: Zum Geburtstag backen wir eine Torte.
torte.context_translation: We are baking a cake for the birthday.
torte.etymology_derivation: Torte — 15th century, from Middle French tarte and tourte, later reinforced by Italian torta, from Late Latin torta (round loaf); English torte was borrowed back from German. [wiktionary]

brötchen.context_phrase: Ich kaufe jeden Morgen frische Brötchen.
brötchen.context_translation: I buy fresh rolls every morning.
brötchen.etymology_derivation: Brötchen — diminutive of Brot (bread), which is cognate with English bread; both trace to PIE *bʰrewh₁-, the root of brew. [wiktionary]

toast.etymology_derivation: Toast — borrowed straight from English toast, with toasten and Toaster as later German offshoots. [wiktionary]

malen.etymology_derivation: From Mal 'spot, mark'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
